content:
Though it’s a choice, it’s not necessary to install something like nginx to host a website on OpenBSD. You can do that with a few tools that already comes with the system.

Get to know the tools

  • httpd(8) , HTTP Daemon, sort of like the Apache HTTP server .
  • relayd(8) , Relay Daemon, works as a reverse proxy.
  • pf(4) , Packet Filter, OpenBSD equivalent of ufw .

If you’re hosting a static website with only HTML, CSS and optionally JavaScript, httpd is all you need (It also supports FastCGI). But if you want a reverse proxy (i.e. forwarding requests to a service with a backend), it’s best to use relayd.

Either way, you need to work with pf. OpenBSD is a proactively secure system that drops most traffic by default. You need to allow ports you need for hosting, usually 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS and 22 for SSH.

httpd and relayd can work together. See httpd as a regular backend to which relayd forwards certain requests.

You’ll also want to work with acme-client(1) for SSL/TLS certificates. Don’t worry. It’s pretty simple. Just a little bit more config than Caddy.

Understand the example httpd.conf

Let’s say you have an index.html file like this.

<p>cool website coming soon...</p>

And you want people to access it via the web. First, you’ll put it somewhere in the system, typically /var/www on Linux systems, but on OpenBSD, you have to put it there.

On OpenBSD, chroot is used for isolation, which means “Change root directory”. httpd’s default chroot directory is /var/www. It means httpd cannot read or write files outside that directory. /var/www is / to httpd process. So if you put your files anywhere else, httpd won’t be able to find it.

Let’s say you put it at /var/www/coolsite/index.html.

Now you need to modify /etc/httpd.conf. You can read an example first:

$ cat /etc/examples/httpd.conf
# $OpenBSD: httpd.conf,v 1.23 2025/02/21 10:19:52 mbuhl Exp $

server "example.com" {
	listen on * port 80
	location "/.well-known/acme-challenge/*" {
		root "/acme"
		request strip 2
	}
	location * {
		block return 302 "https://$HTTP_HOST$REQUEST_URI"
	}
}

server "example.com" {
	listen on * tls port 443
	tls {
		certificate "/etc/ssl/example.com.fullchain.pem"
		key "/etc/ssl/private/example.com.key"
	}
	location "/pub/*" {
		directory auto index
	}
}

The example includes two server blocks. One listens on port 80 of any address (*). The other one listens to TLS traffic on port 443 of any address. These two port numbers are standard TCP ports assgined specifically to HTTP and HTTPS.

HTTP clients (for example, web browsers) establish HTTP connection by sending data to the server’s 80 port, or 443 for HTTPS. Here on the server side, you listen to those ports.

Of course you can listen to other ports like 8080, and then have relayd forward them to from 80/443, which we won’t get into today.

Let’s ignore tls for now. Inside the server blocks, you can typically find location directives. It’s used for specifying rules under a certain location and the paths are matched using shell globbing rules (most commonly *, the wildcard). For example:

location * {
 block return 302 "https://$HTTP_HOST$REQUEST_URI"
}

This means, for any location, return HTTP status code 302 and redirect to https:// URLs. This is common practive for the modern web. Everyone uses HTTPS instead of insecure HTTP. Normally you’ll want to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.

In the HTTPS server block:

location "/pub/*" {
 directory auto index
}

It only specifys rules for /pub/*, so https://example.com/pub/foo will use this rule, but not for .../pub/ or .../pub/foo/bar.

directory is an option for, well, directory. When set to auto index, httpd generates a list of files under certain directory on your file system. By default this is turned off. Most of the time you don’t want to make a directory public.

The default root directory is /htdocs, which is actually /var/www/htdocs (remember chroot?). So the example configuration basically:

  1. Sets up an HTTP server that redirects to https:// URLs
  2. Sets up an HTTPS server that serves files under /var/www/htdocs with directory automatically generated, so all documents under /htdocs are made public

To serve your /var/www/coolsite/index.html, specify root:

- location "/pub/*" {
- directory auto index
- }
+
+ location * {
+ root /coolsite
+ }

You can run httpd -n to check if configuration is valid.

Secure your website

If I had to be honest, a static website does not need Transport Layer Security, literally. Everything is public and the website does not receive let alone process user data. But the modern web decides that everyone should have the same threat model, so here we are. Suck it up and get yourself a TLS certificate.

ℹ️

It had been pointed out to me that it’s possible to inject ads and censor content without TLS/SSL if your ISP has evil intentions. I stand corrected.

Luckily you can use acme-client to automate that, first you need to create /etc/acme-client.conf. Refer to the example here:

$ cat /etc/examples/acme-client.conf
#
# $OpenBSD: acme-client.conf,v 1.6 2025/08/18 15:51:57 job Exp $
#
authority letsencrypt {
	api url "https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"
	account key "/etc/acme/letsencrypt-privkey.pem"
}

authority letsencrypt-staging {
	api url "https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"
	account key "/etc/acme/letsencrypt-staging-privkey.pem"
}

domain example.com {
	alternative names { secure.example.com }
	domain key "/etc/ssl/private/example.com.key"
	domain full chain certificate "/etc/ssl/example.com.fullchain.pem"
	# Test with the staging server to avoid aggressive rate-limiting.
	#sign with letsencrypt-staging
	sign with letsencrypt
}

authority is the big man who signs your certificate so you are allowed on the web. Well, not exactly. Some of them think 4 is a secure enough private key, so let’s not give them too much credit.

Let’s Encrypt is the kind sir that provides free TLS certificates for everyone. It’s the default authority of acme-client and many certificate tools.

Certificate is really just a public key by another name. TLS is an encryption protocol for many things, most commonly HTTPS. SSL (Secure Socket Layer) is the predecessor to TLS, whose name is now used somehow interchangeably in most context.

If you don’t know what a public key is, it’s a part of asymmetric encryption where there are two different keys, the public key and the secret key. The secret key should be stored securely on the server, and the public key is sent to anyone who visits the website as a certificate, so they can verify you’re really who you claim you’re and the connection is not being eavesdropped or attacked by a man in the middle.

To ask for an certificate, precisely a key pair, with acme-client, simply change example.com in the example configuration to your domain, like this:

domain cool.site {
	alternative names { www.cool.site } # <- this is optional
	domain key "/etc/ssl/private/cool.site.key"
	domain full chain certificate "/etc/ssl/cool.site.fullchain.pem"
	sign with letsencrypt
}

Make sure you’ve set up a DNS record that points to this server. Also make sure, /.well-known/acme-client is served through HTTP, so the authority can verify this is actually you that is requesting a certificate.

server "cool.site" {
	listen on * port 80
	location "/.well-known/acme-challenge/*" {
		root "/acme" # acme-client generates files at /var/www/acme
		request strip 2
	}
	location * {
		block return 302 "https://$HTTP_HOST$REQUEST_URI"
	}
}

Run httpd -n to check configuration. If it’s OK, run doas rcctl enable httpd and doas rcctl start httpd to start httpd. If it’s already enabled and started, run doas rcctl reload httpd to reload configuration.1

Then, run this command:

doas acme-client -v cool.site

-v is for verbose operation, which is needed when doing acme challenge on this server for a specific domain for the first time.

The challenge should be completed soon. After that, your certificate and private key will be generated in /etc/ssl and /etc/ssl/private.

Lastly, tell httpd to use those keys.

server "cool.site" {
	listen on * tls port 443
	tls {
		certificate "/etc/ssl/cool.site.fullchain.pem"
		key "/etc/ssl/private/cool.site.key"
	}
 ...
}

And you know what to do:

  1. httpd -n
  2. doas rcctl reload httpd

Then you should be able to visit https://cool.site.

Common Issues

Most commonly something went wrong when you’re running acme-client.

First check if your DNS records are working.

dig cool.site

The output should point to your server.

If DNS records are fine, but traffic fails to go through to your server, chances are they have been dropped by pf.

Edit (as root) /etc/pf.conf, make sure they allow 80 and 443. The following example is from httpd.rocks .

pass in on any proto tcp from any to any port {80 443} keep state \
 (max-src-conn 100, max-src-conn-rate 30/5, overload <block_table> flush global)
pass out on any proto tcp from any to any port {80 443} keep state

table <block_table> persist
block in quick from <block_table>

# Connection limits
set limit states 100000 # Maximum state table entries
set timeout interval 10 # Interval between state purges
set optimization "normal" # General optimization for connection tracking

Before you reload pf, check the syntax. If the following command gives empty output, you’re good to go. If not, don’t reload or your SSH connection might be blocked.

pfctl -nf /etc/pf.conf

And then:

pfctl -f /etc/pf.conf

Automatically renew certificates

On a Unix system, the best way to automate stuff is of course cron, instead of creating a new tool bloated with features just for convenience.

Run doas crontab -e:

3 * * * acme-client cool.site && rcctl reload httpd

This cron job runs every 3 months, request a new certificate and reload httpd. To check if it’s set up, run doas crontab -l.

Summary

Using basic tools instead of Docker and Caddy exposes a lot of technical details that may seem overwhelming. But it’s fun and a good way to learn.

I don’t like magic that hides all the details. I want to know what’s going on underneath. For complex tech issues, just take baby steps and we’ll get there eventually.

No need to rush. Just chill.

See also: httpd.rocks and man httpd.

  1. rcctl is a command line tool to control rc (Run command), which is systemd equivalent on OpenBSD if you’re coming from Linux. If you don’t know what systemd is, it and rc are service managers that manage lifecycles of processes and starts services automatically after reboot. ↩︎
